subject: forensic-medicine
title: Lacerations, Split Lacerations and Incised Wounds

steps.title: A laceration is a blunt tear
steps.tx: A **laceration** is a tear or split of skin, mucosa, muscle or internal organs produced when blunt force crushes or stretches tissue beyond its elasticity. Blows from blunt objects, falls on hard surfaces, machinery and traffic accidents cause them. Localised tissue is displaced by impact, traction forces build, and the tissue rips. Most lacerations need a firm base such as bone acting as an anvil under the skin.
steps.say: Blunt force tears tissue past its elastic limit, usually by pinning skin against bone, and that tear is a laceration.

steps.title: Split lacerations over bone
steps.tx: Crushing skin between two hard objects produces a **split laceration**, the classic scalp wound where tissue is trapped between skull and ground or a blunt weapon. Splits are not undermined, and they show tissue bridges in their depths. One blow over the side of the head can split skin at the parietal prominence, the ear and the jaw together. The surrounding margins usually carry abrasion and bruising from the flatter part of the weapon.
steps.say: Skin crushed against skull splits open like a burst seam, bridges and all, which is why scalp wounds mislead beginners.

nodes.label: Skin splits along the crush line

steps.title: Incised looking lacerations, the great mimic
steps.tx: Over the scalp, eyebrows, cheek bones, jaw, iliac crest, perineum and shin, skin lies so close to bone that blunt splitting yields an **incised looking wound** with deceptively sharp margins. A fall on a flexed knee or elbow, broken glass or a sharp stone can do the same. The giveaway lies in the depth: bridging fibres, crushed hair bulbs and marginal bruising betray blunt force however clean the edge appears.
steps.say: A sharp looking edge over bone can still be blunt, so judge the wound by its bridges and bruising, not its edge.

right.title: True incised wound
points: Any site, made by an edge

steps.title: Stretch, avulsion and tear lacerations
steps.tx: Three further patterns complete the family. **Stretch lacerations** follow overstretching of fixed skin and peel a flap that can point along the direction of a running over vehicle. **Avulsion** shears skin off its attachments by grinding force, called flaying when a lorry wheel strips a limb. Plain **tears** come from irregular semi sharp objects such as car door handles and run deeper at the start than at the end.
steps.say: Stretch peels a flap, avulsion shears skin off its base, and a simple tear starts deep where the object first caught.

steps.title: Tissue bridges settle the diagnosis
steps.tx: The single most reliable sign inside any open wound is the **tissue bridge**: strands of nerve, vessel and elastic fibre that survive in the depth because tissues of different strength tear at different rates. Lacerations show them; incised wounds never do, because a blade divides everything cleanly. Hair bulbs are crushed in laceration and cut in incised wounds, and foreign matter such as grit is commonly driven into a laceration.
steps.say: Bridging strands across the depth prove blunt tearing, since a blade would have divided every strand in its path.

steps.title: Why lacerations bleed less, except on the scalp
steps.tx: Crushed and irregularly torn arteries retract and clot quickly, so **haemorrhage from a laceration** is usually slight compared with a clean cut of the same depth. The scalp breaks the rule: its temporal arteries are bound down firmly in dense tissue, cannot contract, and bleed freely. Multiple skin lacerations can still combine to cause shock and death, and laceration of an internal organ can bleed fatally into a cavity.
steps.say: Torn vessels seal themselves better than cut ones, except in the scalp where bound down arteries keep bleeding.

steps.title: Characters of a true incised wound
steps.tx: An **incised wound** is a clean cut from a sharp edged instrument such as a knife, razor or sickle, and it is longer than it is deep. Margins are clean cut, well defined and usually everted, free of bruising and abrasion. The wound is spindle shaped from central retraction, wider than the blade that made it, and it bleeds profusely because vessels are sliced open and cannot contract when completely divided.
steps.say: A true cut is longer than deep, clean edged, spindle shaped and bleeds freely because sliced vessels cannot close.

steps.title: Head and tail of an incised wound
steps.tx: Pressure is greatest where the blade first bites, so an incised wound is deepest at its start, the **head of the wound**, and shallows toward its end. As the knife leaves the skin it scores a superficial scratch called **tailing of the wound**. Tailing therefore points along the direction of the cut. A blade entering obliquely bevels one margin and undermines the other, showing the side from which the blade approached.
steps.say: Deep head and shallow tailing end show both the direction of the cut and where the blade first struck.

nodes.label: Blade bites deepest at the head

steps.title: Circumstances written in wound patterns
steps.tx: Combinations tell the story: the same weapon can bruise with one blow, lacerate with the next and abrade with a third under **combined blunt injury patterns**. Punching splits lips and blackens eyes; kicking and stamping add footwear patterns and can fracture ribs or injure abdominal organs through the body wall. Homicidal lacerations favour the head. Suicidal lacerations are rare, exposed and mostly on the same side of the body.
steps.say: Mixed abrasion, bruise and tear patterns plus their sites separate punching, stamping, falls and homicidal blows.
